WAGE REPAYMENT / CLAWBACK — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · Acme Corp.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This is an informational sheet about California Labor Code §§ 221-224 — the statutes that limit an employer's ability to collect back, or withhold, wages already paid to an employee — prepared in connection with a payment made or promised by Acme Corp. to Jane Doe: signing bonus repayable if employment ends within 12 months. Amount at issue: $5,000.

This document explains, using the statutes' own text, what California law says (and does not say) about an employer collecting back wages already paid, the statutes' own narrow exception for certain deductions, and the separate question of whether California law specifically addresses recouping a signing bonus, relocation payment, or training cost after early departure. It is informational only. It does not determine whether $5,000, or any part of it, is lawfully owed, collectible, or deductible in this or any other specific case, does not determine which state's law applies, and is not a substitute for advice from a qualified attorney.

THE CORE RULE: AN EMPLOYER CANNOT COLLECT BACK WAGES ALREADY PAID
California Labor Code § 221 makes it unlawful for an employer to collect or receive back any part of wages it has already paid to an employee. The statute is a single, general sentence — it does not single out signing bonuses, relocation payments, training costs, or any other specific category of payment, and the words "repayment," "clawback," "chargeback," and "training repayment agreement" appear nowhere in its text. Whatever a specific payment to Jane Doe is called by Acme Corp., § 221's prohibition applies to it once, and only once, that payment has actually become wages already paid to Jane Doe — a threshold question this section's own text does not answer for any particular payment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "It shall be unlawful for any employer to collect or receive from an employee any part of wages theretofore paid by said employer to said employee."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 221 (California Legislative Information text), the prohibition on collecting back wages already paid (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=221.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, quoted from its own current text — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific payment, and not a claim that § 221 applies (or does not apply) to any specific signing bonus, relocation payment, or training-cost arrangement. This is a single, self-contained statutory section with no lettered subdivisions; no additional independent source was needed to confirm its internal structure. The statute's own text does not define which payments count as "wages theretofore paid" for its purposes, and in particular does not say whether a signing bonus, relocation payment, or training cost is, by its nature, a wage rather than something else (such as a loan or an advance) — that distinction has instead been addressed by California courts and, separately, by Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (DLSE) opinion letters, addressed honestly and separately in this document's companion clauses rather than folded into this one.

TWO RELATED, BUT NARROWER, PROHIBITIONS — §§ 222 AND 223
In the same chapter as § 221, two other Labor Code sections prohibit related but distinct conduct. Section 222 makes it unlawful, specifically "in case of any wage agreement arrived at through collective bargaining," to withhold any part of the agreed wage willfully, unlawfully, or with intent to defraud an employee, a competitor, or any other person. Section 223 makes it unlawful, where a statute or contract requires an employer to maintain a designated wage scale, to secretly pay a lower wage while purporting to pay the designated one. Neither section, on its own text, is written around a departing employee's signing bonus, relocation payment, or training cost: § 222 requires a collective-bargaining wage agreement and a showing of willfulness, unlawfulness, or intent to defraud, and § 223 requires a statute or contract that designates a wage scale and a secret underpayment against it — facts that are not present in most bonus, relocation, or training-repayment arrangements, though whether they are present in Jane Doe's specific arrangement with Acme Corp. is not something this clause determines.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "It shall be unlawful, in case of any wage agreement arrived at through collective bargaining, either wilfully or unlawfully or with intent to defraud an employee, a competitor, or any other person, to withhold from said employee any part of the wage agreed upon."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 222 (California Legislative Information text), the collective-bargaining wage-withholding prohibition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=222.)
  "Where any statute or contract requires an employer to maintain the designated wage scale, it shall be unlawful to secretly pay a lower wage while purporting to pay the wage designated by statute or by contract."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 223 (California Legislative Information text), the secret-underpayment-against-a-designated-wage-scale prohibition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=223.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, quoted from its own current text for two independently numbered sections (§ 222 and § 223) within the same chapter as § 221 — they are genuinely separate statutory provisions, not subdivisions of one section or of § 221 itself, though this clause treats them together because both are narrower, fact-specific prohibitions rather than the general rule stated in § 221. Each is a single, self-contained section with no lettered subdivisions. This clause does not determine whether any collective-bargaining wage agreement or any statute or contract designating a wage scale exists in a specific reader's situation, and does not claim that § 222 or § 223 is either satisfied or foreclosed by any particular signing-bonus, relocation, or training-repayment provision.

THE STATUTE'S OWN EXCEPTION — § 224
Sections 221, 222, and 223 are not absolute: Labor Code § 224 states that none of them makes it unlawful for an employer to withhold or divert part of an employee's wages in three specific circumstances stated on the statute's own face — (1) when the employer is required or empowered to do so by state or federal law; (2) when a deduction is expressly authorized in writing by the employee to cover insurance premiums, hospital or medical dues, or other deductions not amounting to a rebate or deduction from the standard wage arrived at by collective bargaining or pursuant to a wage agreement or statute; or (3) when a deduction to cover health and welfare or pension plan contributions is expressly authorized by a collective bargaining or wage agreement. Section 224 separately makes clear that nothing in it authorizes an employer to withhold or divert wages to pay any tax, fee, or charge prohibited by Government Code § 50026, regardless of whether the employee has authorized it. Section 224's own text does not list a signing bonus, relocation payment, or training cost as a fourth qualifying category, and does not say that a separately signed repayment agreement automatically satisfies category (2)'s "expressly authorized in writing" language for a deduction of that kind.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The provisions of Sections 221, 222 and 223 shall in no way make it unlawful for an employer to withhold or divert any portion of an employee’s wages when the employer is required or empowered so to do by state or federal law or when a deduction is expressly authorized in writing by the employee to cover insurance premiums, hospital or medical dues, or other deductions not amounting to a rebate or deduction from the standard wage arrived at by collective bargaining or pursuant to wage agreement or statute, or when a deduction to cover health and welfare or pension plan contributions is expressly authorized by a collective bargaining or wage agreement. Nothing in this section or any other provision of law shall be construed as authorizing an employer to withhold or divert any portion of an employee’s wages to pay any tax, fee or charge prohibited by Section 50026 of the Government Code, whether or not the employee authorizes such withholding or diversion."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 224 (California Legislative Information text), the exception for legally required, individually authorized, and collectively bargained deductions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=224.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, quoted in full from its own current text — a single statutory section with no lettered subdivisions of its own (the numbering (1)-(3) above is this drafter's organization of the section's one long sentence, not the Legislature's own subdivision lettering), so the full text is quoted as one contiguous passage below rather than split into separately cited subdivisions. This clause does not independently fetch or verify the text of Government Code § 50026, which § 224 cross-references only to disclaim authorizing withholding to pay a prohibited tax, fee, or charge; only the fact and wording of that cross-reference is stated here. Section 224's text does not resolve, and this clause does not determine, whether a specific signed repayment agreement for a signing bonus, relocation payment, or training cost would qualify as a category-(2) deduction "expressly authorized in writing by the employee" and "not amounting to a rebate" — that is a fact-specific application of the statute's general language that no independently verified case law or DLSE guidance in this clause set resolves directly.

HOW COURTS HAVE READ "WAGES ALREADY PAID"
California courts applying § 221 have read its prohibition on collecting back "wages" as reaching only wages that have actually been earned by the employee's performance of whatever the payment's own terms required — not a payment that was, by its own terms, merely a conditional advance against something not yet earned. This is the same statutory language and the same judicial gloss already addressed, in the different setting of a commission chargeback, by this corpus's separate Commission Payout Upon Termination document; it is restated here because it bears directly on a signing bonus, relocation payment, or training-cost repayment as well. Whether § 221 protects a specific payment to Jane Doe from being collected back therefore depends on whether that payment was, by its own terms, already earned when Acme Corp. paid it — a question this judicial gloss identifies but does not answer for any particular signing bonus, relocation payment, or training-repayment arrangement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "In referring to “wages” paid, section 221 prohibits an employer only from collecting or receiving wages that have already been earned by performance of agreed-upon requirements."
  — Steinhebel v. Los Angeles Times Communications, LLC, 126 Cal. App. 4th 696, 707 (2005) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2259299/steinhebel-v-los-angeles-times-commun/)
  Known gap: This is one state's case law, used as real evidence of how a California Court of Appeal has read § 221's "wages already paid" language — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific payment, and not a claim that any particular signing bonus, relocation payment, or training-repayment provision was or was not already earned. This exact quotation was independently verified against the opinion's primary text by an earlier session of this project (for this corpus's Commission Payout Upon Termination document, clause id commpayout_forfeiture_unlawful) and is reused verbatim here rather than re-fetched this session: this session's CourtListener MCP tool returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response (125 requests/day, quota not resetting until after this session ends), a direct curl fetch of the opinion's page on courtlistener.com returned an AWS WAF "challenge" response (HTTP 202 with an empty body, not the opinion text), and the WebFetch tool reported that the courtlistener.com domain itself is blocked by this environment's network egress proxy (error type EGRESS_BLOCKED) — all three access paths were tried and all three failed, so this citation is disclosed as reused-and-previously-verified rather than independently re-verified this session. Separately, and more importantly for this clause set's specific topic: Steinhebel was a commission-chargeback case, not a case about a signing bonus, relocation payment, or training-repayment agreement; no case squarely addressing the recoupment of a signing bonus, relocation payment, or training cost was independently verified against a primary source this session (see this document's companion clause on DLSE opinion letters for what non-statutory agency guidance, as distinct from independently verified case law, says about a closely related bonus-repayment scenario).

AGENCY GUIDANCE, NOT THE STATUTE: DLSE OPINION LETTERS
Separately from the statute's own text, the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (DLSE) — the state agency that enforces the Labor Code's wage provisions — has addressed an employer's bonus-repayment provision directly in at least one opinion letter, and has described the legal weight of its own opinion letters in another. Responding in 1987 to an employer's proposed policy of requiring an already-paid bonus to be repaid if the employee did not remain employed for a full year, DLSE's Chief Counsel identified two problems with the proposal: first, that structuring an annual bonus as quarterly payments subject to repayment raises the question of whether the bonus was actually earned quarterly rather than annually; and second, that two California court decisions, described in the letter only by short name and not independently verified in this clause set, "can be interpreted to prevent an employer from deducting the amount of the bonus from any wages due" — meaning an employer wanting the bonus back would have to pursue the employee through the civil courts rather than simply withholding it from wages. Separately, in a 1993 letter on a different bonus question, DLSE described the weight its own opinion letters carry: an "official opinion" by the Division "would be entitled to little or no weight in the courts," because interpreting bonus contracts is not an area the Legislature has given DLSE authority to set binding standards. Neither letter is the statute itself, and neither is a court decision; both are the agency's own non-binding interpretive guidance about bonus repayment specifically, offered here because Jane Doe or Acme Corp. may encounter this kind of guidance cited elsewhere as though it settled the question.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Paying a yearly bonus on a quarterly basis would not be violative of any of the State’s wage payment laws; however, requiring the quarterly bonus to be repaid if the employee does not remain for one year presents several problems."
  — Cal. Dep't of Indus. Relations, Div. of Labor Standards Enforcement, Opinion Letter 1987.07.01 (bonus repayment upon early termination), DLSE Opinion Letter 1987.07.01 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/opinions/1987-07-01.pdf)
  "The second problem with your concept is the application of two court decisions, Kerr's Catering and Barnhill, which can be interpreted to prevent an employer from deducting the amount of the bonus from any wages due."
  — Cal. Dep't of Indus. Relations, Div. of Labor Standards Enforcement, Opinion Letter 1987.07.01 (bonus repayment upon early termination), DLSE Opinion Letter 1987.07.01 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/opinions/1987-07-01.pdf)
  "Any "official opinion" by this Division would be entitled to little or no weight in the courts."
  — Cal. Dep't of Indus. Relations, Div. of Labor Standards Enforcement, Opinion Letter 1993.01.19 (bonuses to terminated employees), DLSE Opinion Letter 1993.01.19 (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/opinions/1993-01-19.pdf)
  Known gap: These are two DLSE opinion letters, fetched directly from dir.ca.gov/dlse/opinions and independently verified this session — each PDF was fetched twice, using two distinct User-Agent strings, and the two fetches were byte-identical for both letters. Both are non-binding agency guidance, not statutes and not court decisions; the 1993 letter's own text says so explicitly, in the language quoted above, about DLSE opinion letters generally. The 1987 letter's reference to two court decisions (given in the letter only as "Kerr's Catering and Barnhill," without a full citation) is reported here only as the letter's own characterization of those cases; this clause does not independently verify either case's citation or holding, for the same CourtListener rate-limiting and blocked-network-access reasons disclosed in this document's companion clause on the § 221 judicial gloss. The 1987 letter concerns a quarterly-versus-annual bonus repayment scenario specifically, not a signing bonus, relocation payment, or training-repayment agreement by name; no DLSE opinion letter specifically addressing a signing bonus, relocation cost, or training-repayment agreement by that name was found in DLSE's own opinion-letter index (searched by subject at dir.ca.gov/dlse/OpinionLetters-bySubject.htm) during this session's research, and this clause does not assume one exists. A separate, related 1993 DLSE letter in the same index addresses a different question — whether a bonus not yet paid must be paid at all when an employee voluntarily leaves before a vesting date — rather than clawing back a bonus already paid, and is not addressed in this clause set.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF RECEIPT
Jane Doe acknowledges receiving this informational sheet about California Labor Code §§ 221-224 in connection with the payment described above. This acknowledgment confirms only that Jane Doe received and reviewed this sheet. It is not an agreement about whether $5,000, or any part of it, is owed, collectible, or deductible, and it does not waive any right or defense Jane Doe or Acme Corp. may have.
